citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$,
let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift as in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose it is
$L^2$-$m$-approximable. Write $\sigma=(\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$,
let $S_1(H)$ be the trace-class Banach space with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]),
write $\mathbb E_B$ for a Bochner integral, and define $x\otimes y:H\to H$ by
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_Hx$. The Bochner series
$$ \Gamma=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0]+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j] +\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\bigr) $$
converges absolutely in trace norm to a positive self-adjoint trace-class
operator. For $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$, the Bochner covariance operators
$\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$ satisfy
$\|\Gamma_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. If $\boxtimes$ is the product-kernel class from
[[lem-real-l-two-kernel-operator-is-bounded-and-rank-one-compatible]], then
$$ \kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes X_j],\qquad \widetilde\kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_j\boxtimes X_0] $$
are well-defined elements of $K=L^2([0,1]^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$, and
$$ c=\kappa_0+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\kappa_j+\widetilde\kappa_j) $$
converges absolutely in $K$ and satisfies $T_c=\Gamma$. Equivalently, $c$ is
the design's long-run covariance-kernel series interpreted as an
$L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class; no pointwise representatives are fixed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space and let $(e_k)$ be a finite or countable
orthonormal family whose finite linear span is dense in $H$. Here
orthonormal means $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_H=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise;
density means every $x\in H$ is arbitrarily close in norm to a finite linear
combination of the $e_k$. For $x\in H$, define
$$P_Nx=\sum_{k\le N}\langle x,e_k\rangle_H e_k,$$
using all basis vectors once $N$ reaches the size of a finite family. Then
$P_Nx\to x$ in norm and
$$\|x\|_H^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a fixed complete finite or countable
orthonormal basis $(e_k)$. On a probability
space let $U,V$ be independent, strongly measurable and Bochner-integrable
$H$-valued random elements with
$\mathbb E_B U=\mathbb E_B V=0$ and
$\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2,\mathbb E\|V\|_H^2<\infty$. Then
$$\mathbb E\langle U,V\rangle_H=0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$ be finite integers, and let $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered strictly stationary sequence of $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|Y_0\|^2<\infty$. Strict stationarity means that every finite-dimensional law is invariant under integer shifts. Assume $m$-dependence: for each $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(Y_t)_{t\le a}$ and $(Y_t)_{t\ge a+m+1}$ are independent, in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Set
$$\Sigma_m=\sum_{|j|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_j),$$
where $\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=\mathbb E[(U-\mathbb EU)(V-\mathbb EV)^T]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Then $\Sigma_m$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,\Sigma_m).$$
The conclusion allows singular $\Sigma_m$, including $\Sigma_m=0$.

Assume AC. For Borel probability laws $\mu_n$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$,
$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Random elements $X_n,X$ with values in the same metric space **converge in distribution**, written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their laws from [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] satisfy $P_{X_n}\Rightarrow P_X$ in [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]. They may be defined on different probability spaces. The definition specifies only their marginal laws.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

derivations.claim: Put $\sigma=\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}$ and $D_{t,m}=X_t-X_{t,m}$ for $m\ge1$. Both terms have the same centered law, so $D_{t,m}$ is centered. For $h\ge1$, $X_{h,h}$ is independent of $D_{0,m}$: its original inputs have indices $1,\ldots,h$, while $D_{0,m}$ uses original indices at most $0$ and its own replacement array; $X_{h,h}$ uses a distinct independent replacement array. It has the centered law of $X_0$, so [F10] gives $\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,h}\rangle_H=0$. Also $\|X_h-X_{h,h}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_h$. Hence Cauchy--Schwarz gives $$|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_h\rangle_H| =|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_h-X_{h,h}\rangle_H| \le\delta_m\delta_h.$$ If $h\ge m$, the original inputs of $X_{h,m}$ have indices $h-m+1,\ldots,h$, all positive, and its replacement array is independent of the coordinates in $D_{0,m}$; hence it is independent of $D_{0,m}$ and centered. [F10] gives $\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,m}\rangle_H=0$. If $1\le h<m$, its marginal second moment is $\sigma^2$, giving $|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},X_{h,m}\rangle_H|\le\delta_m\sigma$. Therefore $$|\mathbb E\langle D_{0,m},D_{h,m}\rangle_H| \le\begin{cases}\delta_m(\delta_h+\sigma),&1\le h<m,\\ \delta_m\delta_h,&h\ge m.\end{cases}$$ Stationarity makes the negative-lag inner products equal to the corresponding positive-lag ones. Expanding the squared norm of the normalized sum and bounding each finite-lag weight by one yields, for $U_n=n^{-1/2}S_n$ and $U_n^{(m)}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^nX_{t,m}$, $$\sup_n\mathbb E\|U_n-U_n^{(m)}\|_H^2 \le\delta_m^2+2\delta_m\sum_{h\ge1}\delta_h+2\sigma(m-1)\delta_m.$$ The $m=1$ empty middle-lag sum is zero.

Since $\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty$, $\liminf_{m\to\infty}m\delta_m=0$: otherwise $\delta_m\ge c/m$ eventually for some $c>0$, contradicting summability. Recursively choose strictly increasing integers $m_r$ with $m_r\delta_{m_r}<1/r$; the least eligible integer at each stage exists by the liminf statement. Thus the right side of step 1.1 tends to zero along $m=m_r$. Write $\varepsilon_m$ for its square root. For each fixed $K$, the covariance matrices of $P_KU_n$ are bounded because $\operatorname{Cov}(U_n)=\Gamma_n$ and [F2] bounds $\operatorname{tr}(P_K\Gamma_nP_K)$. For any $v\in P_KH$, the scalar variance difference satisfies $$|\mathbb E\langle U_n^{(m)}-\mathbb EU_n^{(m)},v\rangle_H^2 -\mathbb E\langle U_n,v\rangle_H^2| \le\|v\|_H^2\varepsilon_m(2M_K+\varepsilon_m),$$ where $M_K=\sup_n(\mathbb E\|P_KU_n\|_H^2)^{1/2}<\infty$; this follows from $|a^2-b^2|\le|a-b|(|a|+|b|)$ and [F9].

For fixed $m$ and $K$, the coordinate vectors $(\langle X_{t,m},e_1\rangle_H,\ldots,\langle X_{t,m},e_K\rangle_H)_t$ are centered, stationary, $m$-dependent and square-integrable in $\mathbb R^K$; they identify $P_KX_{t,m}$ isometrically with $P_KH$. By [F4], their normalized sums converge to a centered Gaussian with covariance matrix $\Sigma_{m,K}=\sum_{|j|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(P_KX_{0,m},P_KX_{j,m})$. The finite covariance expansion shows $\operatorname{Cov}(P_KU_n^{(m)})=\sum_{|j|\le m}(1-|j|/n)_+\, \operatorname{Cov}(P_KX_{0,m},P_KX_{j,m})\to\Sigma_{m,K}$; terms with $|j|>m$ vanish by $m$-dependence, and each of the finitely many coefficients tends to one. Letting $n\to\infty$ in step 2.1 and using [F2] gives $$\|\Sigma_{m,K}-P_K\Gamma P_K\|_{op} \le\varepsilon_m(2M_K+\varepsilon_m).$$ In particular $\Sigma_{m_r,K}\to P_K\Gamma P_K$. Because these operators are symmetric and finite-dimensional, their operator norm is the supremum of the absolute quadratic form over unit vectors. For each real $v\in P_KH$, [F11] therefore gives convergence of the characteristic functions of the scalar projections of $N(0,\Sigma_{m_r,K})$ to that of $N(0,P_K\Gamma P_K)$; [F5] and Cramér--Wold give convergence of these finite-dimensional Gaussian laws.

For $a\in P_KH$, compare the characteristic functions of $\langle U_n,a\rangle_H$ and $\langle U_n^{(m)},a\rangle_H$. The inequality $|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|\le|x-y|$ and step 1.1 bound their difference by $\|a\|_H\varepsilon_m$. For each fixed $m$, [F4] gives the limit law of the second projection; along $m=m_r$, step 3.1 and [F11] make those Gaussian limit laws converge to $N(0,\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle_H)$. Taking first $n\to\infty$ and then $r\to\infty$ proves convergence of the characteristic functions of $\langle U_n,a\rangle_H$ to that normal law. Explicitly, their limsup difference from the target characteristic function is at most $$\|a\|_H\varepsilon_m+ \left|e^{-\langle\Sigma_{m,K}a,a\rangle_H/2} -e^{-\langle\Gamma a,a\rangle_H/2}\right|,$$ which tends to zero along $m=m_r$ by steps 1.1 and 3.1. Since $a$ ranges over all vectors, for any fixed projection direction $b$ this also gives its characteristic-function convergence at every frequency $t$ by taking $a=tb$. Thus [F5] and Cramér--Wold give $$P_KU_n\Rightarrow P_KG$$ for every fixed $K$, since $G$ has covariance $\Gamma$.

Let $R_K=I-P_K$ and $\alpha_K=(\mathbb E\|R_KX_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. Completeness of the eigenbasis and Parseval give $R_KX_0\to0$ almost surely in $H$; the bound $\|R_KX_0\|_H^2\le\|X_0\|_H^2$ and [F6] imply $\alpha_K\to0$. For $h\ge1$, $X_0$ is independent of $X_{h,h-1}$ by [F1]; bounded linear projection preserves independence and centering, so [F10] gives $\mathbb E\langle R_KX_0,R_KX_{h,h-1}\rangle_H=0$. Hence $$|\mathbb E\langle R_KX_0,R_KX_h\rangle_H| =|\mathbb E\langle R_KX_0,R_K(X_h-X_{h,h-1})\rangle_H| \le\alpha_K\delta_{h-1}.$$ Expanding the variance of $R_KU_n$ and using [F9] now gives $$\sup_n\mathbb E\|R_KU_n\|_H^2 \le\alpha_K^2+2\alpha_K\left(\delta_0+\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m\right)\longrightarrow0.$$ Also [F3], [F3a] and the covariance of $G$ give $\mathbb E\|R_KG\|_H^2=\sum_{k>K}\lambda_k\to0$; if the basis is finite, take $P_K=I$ once all basis vectors are included.

Let $\phi:H\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and uniformly continuous, with $M=\sup_x|\phi(x)|$. For $\eta>0$ put $\omega_\phi(\eta)=\sup_{\|x-y\|\le\eta}|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|$, which tends to zero as $\eta\downarrow0$. Markov's inequality [F7] and step 5.1 imply $$|\mathbb E\phi(U_n)-\mathbb E\phi(P_KU_n)| \le\omega_\phi(\eta)+2M\eta^{-2}\sup_n\mathbb E\|R_KU_n\|_H^2,$$ and the same bound for $G$ and $P_KG$ with $\mathbb E\|R_KG\|_H^2$. For fixed $K$, step 4.1 gives $\mathbb E\phi(P_KU_n)\to\mathbb E\phi(P_KG)$. First let $K\to\infty$ in these inequalities and then let $\eta\downarrow0$. It follows that $\mathbb E\phi(U_n)\to\mathbb E\phi(G)$ for every bounded uniformly continuous $\phi$. By [F8], $U_n\Rightarrow G$ in the Borel weak topology of $H$. The kernel assertion is the conclusion of the long-run covariance lemma; the theorem asserts no time-indexed process convergence.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. Every probability measure $\nu$
on $(S,\Sigma)$ is the common law of a countable independent family of
$S$-valued random elements.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: By [F6], the coefficient series $\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)^{-2}$ converges and its tails tend to zero. Therefore at each recursive stage the set of integers larger than the preceding index for which the stated tail is below $2^{-4r}$ is nonempty, so its least member $N_r$ exists. For a deterministic sign sequence $x=(x_k)_{k\ge0}$, put $s_N(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}x_k/(k+1)$. Each $s_N$ is product-measurable. The set on which $(s_{N_r})_{r\ge0}$ is Cauchy is Borel, because the Cauchy condition is a countable combination of inequalities between these measurable real functions. On that set their limit is measurable, and extending it by zero on the complement is product-measurable. Thus $f$ is a total Borel map into the one-dimensional subspace $\mathbb Re\subset H$.

On the given probability space carrying the iid innovations, the partial sums $S_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\epsilon_{-k}/(k+1)$ are Cauchy in $L^2$, since for $M>N$ independence, centering and [F4] give $$\mathbb E|S_M-S_N|^2=\sum_{k=N+1}^{M}(k+1)^{-2}\longrightarrow0.$$ By [F2] they converge in $L^2$ to a random variable $S$. Each $S_N$ has mean zero and squared norm $\|S_N\|_2^2=\sum_{k=0}^N(k+1)^{-2}$; [F5] therefore gives $\mathbb ES=0$ and $\mathbb ES^2=\|S\|_2^2=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}<\infty$ by [F6]. Choose increasing $N_r$ with $\sum_{k>N_r}(k+1)^{-2}<2^{-4r}$. Taking $M\to\infty$ in the finite tail-variance identity gives $\mathbb E|S_{N_r}-S|^2=\sum_{k>N_r}(k+1)^{-2}$. Thus [F3] gives $$P(|S_{N_r}-S|>2^{-r})\le 2^{2r}\mathbb E|S_{N_r}-S|^2<2^{-2r}.$$ These probabilities are summable, so [F3] implies $S_{N_r}\to S$ almost surely. Hence the defining subsequence filter equals $S e$ almost surely. In particular $X_0$ is centered and $$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2=\mathbb ES^2=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}<\infty.$$ The same argument applies to every shifted iid input sequence.

For fixed $m\ge1$, the mixed sequence used by $X_{0,m}$ is itself iid Rademacher, so its filter is the corresponding $L^2$ limit. Subtracting its partial sums from those for $X_0$ cancels the terms $k<m$ and leaves $$X_0-X_{0,m}=e\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_{-k}-\epsilon'_{0,m,-k}}{k+1} \quad\text{in }L^2.$$ The summands are independent, centered, and have variance $2/(k+1)^2$ by [F4]; finite-tail variance computation followed by $L^2$ convergence therefore gives $\delta_m^2=2\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2}$.

Since $x\mapsto x^{-2}$ is decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, $$\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}(k+1)^{-2} \ge\int_{m+1}^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=\frac1{m+1}.$$ Thus $\delta_m\ge\sqrt{2/(m+1)}$, and the decreasing-function integral comparison gives $$\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m\ge\sqrt2\sum_{j\ge2}j^{-1/2}\ge\sqrt2\int_2^{\infty}x^{-1/2}\,dx=+\infty$$ by [F6]. The moment condition holds by step 2.1, but the required dependence-coefficient summability fails.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. Every probability measure $\nu$
on $(S,\Sigma)$ is the common law of a countable independent family of
$S$-valued random elements.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. Every probability measure $\nu$
on $(S,\Sigma)$ is the common law of a countable independent family of
$S$-valued random elements.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.

  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$

  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation

common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$

   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise

2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable

nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence

$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in

[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered

is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$

kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.

derivations.claim: For every input sequence with $|\epsilon_t|=1$, $\sum_{k\ge0}|2^{-k}\epsilon_{t-k}|\le2$, so the series converges absolutely and uniformly over the product space. Its partial sums are product-measurable and bounded by $2$, so their pointwise limit is a Borel causal map. Finite partial-sum variances are $\sum_{k\le N}4^{-k}$ by [F2]; the uniform bound and dominated convergence give centering and $\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2=\sum_{k\ge0}4^{-k}=4/3<\infty$. Dominated convergence [F2] passes these variances to the infinite tail, giving $\delta_m^2=2\sum_{k=m}^\infty4^{-k}=\frac83\,4^{-m}.$ Thus $\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m=\sqrt{8/3}\sum_{m\ge1}2^{-m}<\infty$.

For $j\ge0$, truncate both linear sums at index $N$. Their product is bounded by $4$ and converges pointwise to $X_0X_j$, so dominated convergence [F2] passes expectations to the limit. The finite sums share exactly innovations with indices $-k=j-(k+j)$; their coefficient products are $2^{-k}2^{-(k+j)}$, while all other products have zero expectation by [F2]. The finite shared-coefficient sums tend to $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}2^{-(k+j)}$, giving $\gamma_j=\mathbb E\langle X_0,X_j\rangle_H =\frac43\,2^{-j}.$ Symmetry gives $\gamma_{-j}=\gamma_j$. Therefore the scalar long-run variance is $$\gamma_0+2\sum_{j\ge1}\gamma_j =\frac43+\frac83\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}=4,$$ and the operator is $4(e\otimes e)$.

Step 1.1 gives centering, a finite second moment and summable physical-dependence errors; step 2.1 gives the long-run covariance. Applying [F3] yields convergence of the normalized $H$-valued sums to a centered Gaussian with covariance $4(e\otimes e)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

$$P_Nx=\sum_{k\le N}\langle x,e_k\rangle_H e_k,$$
using all basis vectors once $N$ reaches the size of a finite family. Then
$P_Nx\to x$ in norm and
$$\|x\|_H^2=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{k\le N}|\langle x,e_k\rangle_H|^2.$$

Let $\varepsilon>0$. By density choose a finite linear combination $y$ of the $e_k$ with $\|x-y\|_H<\varepsilon$, and choose $N$ at least as large as every index used in $y$. Then $y$ lies in the first-$N$ span, so step 1.1 gives $\|x-P_Nx\|_H\le\|x-y\|_H<\varepsilon$. Hence $P_Nx\to x$; the first identity in step 1.1 then gives the asserted Parseval limit. For a finite family, $P_Nx=x$ once all its vectors are included.
